summary: Describes how to use the Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (ECDSA) to authenticate peers in IKE and IKEv2. ECDSA can offer faster computation, smaller signatures and lower bandwidth use.

plainLanguage.summary: IKE and IKEv2 are the protocols that set up IPsec connections, and each side has to prove who it is before the connection starts. This RFC adds elliptic curve signatures to the choices, which produce a smaller signature than RSA or DSA for the same level of security.

subtitle: How IKE and IKEv2 can authenticate each other with elliptic curve signatures instead of RSA or DSA.

tldr.problem: IKE and IKEv2 could authenticate their two ends with RSA or DSA signatures, and both of those need more bytes on the wire and more computing time than an elliptic curve signature of the same strength.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines three signature algorithms for IKE and IKEv2, ECDSA-256, ECDSA-384 and ECDSA-521. Each names both the elliptic curve group and the hash function, because IKEv2 has no separate transform type for hashes.
tldr.outcome: IKE and IKEv2 gained ECDSA as an authentication method with no change to the existing operation of the protocol. The three algorithms are registered with IANA.

today: RFC 4754 is a Proposed Standard from January 2007, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It adds three authentication method names to the IPsec and IKEv2 registries and names the elliptic curve groups they use, which are specified in RFC 4753.

sections.title: Adding ECDSA to IKE and IKEv2
sections.content:
The Internet Key Exchange is a key agreement and security negotiation protocol used for key establishment in IPsec. In the initial set of exchanges, both parties must authenticate each other using a negotiated authentication method. In the original version of IKE this occurs in Phase 1, and in IKEv2 it occurs in the exchange called IKE-AUTH.

One option for the authentication method is digital signatures using public key cryptography. Two digital signature methods were defined for use within Phase 1 and IKE-AUTH: RSA signatures and Digital Signature Algorithm signatures. This document introduces ECDSA signatures as a third method.

For any given level of security against the best attacks known, ECDSA signatures are smaller than RSA signatures, and ECDSA keys require less bandwidth than DSA keys. There are also advantages of computational speed and efficiency in many settings. Additional efficiency may be gained by simultaneously using ECDSA for IKE and IKEv2 authentication and elliptic curve groups for the key exchange. This document adds ECDSA capability to IKE and IKEv2 without introducing any changes to existing IKE operation.
sections.plainLanguage: Before a protected connection is set up, the two ends have to show they are who they claim to be. This RFC gives them a third way to do that, using signatures built on elliptic curves, which are shorter than the RSA and DSA signatures that were already available.

sections.title: What ECDSA Is
sections.content:
The Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm is the elliptic curve analogue of the DSA signature method. It is defined in the ANSI X9.62 standard, and other compatible specifications include FIPS 186-2, IEEE 1363, IEEE 1363A and SEC 1.

ECDSA signatures are smaller than RSA signatures of similar cryptographic strength. ECDSA public keys, and the certificates that carry them, are smaller than similar strength DSA keys, which improves communications efficiency. Furthermore, on many platforms ECDSA operations can be computed more quickly than similar strength RSA or DSA operations. These advantages of signature size, bandwidth and computational efficiency may make ECDSA an attractive choice for many IKE and IKEv2 implementations.
sections.plainLanguage: ECDSA is a signature method built on elliptic curves, a branch of mathematics about curves made of numbers. For the same level of protection, the signature and the key are smaller than with RSA or DSA, and on many computers the arithmetic is faster.

sections.title: Naming the Three Signature Algorithms
sections.content:
The IANA-assigned attribute number for authentication using generic ECDSA in IKE is 8, but the corresponding list of IKEv2 authentication methods does not include ECDSA. Moreover, ECDSA cannot be specified for IKEv2 independently of an associated hash function, because IKEv2 does not have a transform type for hash functions. The hash function must therefore be specified as part of the signature algorithm, and the elliptic curve group must be specified as well, since the choice of hash function depends on it.

As a result, three signature algorithms are named: ECDSA-256, ECDSA-384 and ECDSA-521. Each is an instantiation of the ECDSA algorithm using a particular elliptic curve group and hash function. ECDSA-256 uses the 256-bit random ECP group with SHA-256, ECDSA-384 uses the 384-bit random ECP group with SHA-384, and ECDSA-521 uses the 521-bit random ECP group with SHA-512. The elliptic curve groups, including their base points, are specified in RFC 4753. For reasons of consistency, the document defines the signatures for IKE in the same way.
sections.plainLanguage: IKEv2 has no separate slot for naming a hash function, so the hash has to be built into the name of the signature algorithm. That gives three fixed choices, each pairing a curve size with the hash of the same size: 256 with SHA-256, 384 with SHA-384, and 521 with SHA-512.

sections.title: The Signature Encoding
sections.content:
When ECDSA-256, ECDSA-384 or ECDSA-521 is used as the digital signature in IKE or IKEv2, the signature payload shall contain an encoding of the computed signature consisting of the concatenation of a pair of integers r and s. The bit lengths of r and s and the resulting signature are given for each algorithm: ECDSA-256 uses 256-bit values of r and s for a signature of 512 bits, ECDSA-384 uses 384-bit values for a signature of 768 bits, and ECDSA-521 uses 528-bit values for a signature of 1056 bits.

The bit lengths of r and s are enforced, if necessary, by prepending the value with zeros. So a signature always occupies the same number of bytes, whatever the particular numbers happen to be.
sections.plainLanguage: A signature is two numbers, r and s, written one after the other. Each is padded with leading zeros to a fixed length, so the signature is always the same size: 512 bits for ECDSA-256, 768 bits for ECDSA-384 and 1056 bits for ECDSA-521.

sections.title: How a Signature Is Computed and Checked
sections.content:
The test vectors use the Diffie-Hellman group given by the elliptic curve y^2 = (x^3 - 3x + b) modulo p. If (x,y) is a point on the curve, then (x,y)^n denotes the scalar multiple of that point by the integer n, which is another point on the curve. The group order for the curve group is denoted q and the generator is denoted g = (gx, gy). The hash of the message is denoted h. The signer's static private key is denoted w, an integer between zero and q, and the signer's static public key is g^w = (gwx, gwy). The ephemeral private key is denoted k, an integer between zero and q, with ephemeral public key g^k = (gkx, gky). The quantity kinv is the integer between zero and q such that k * kinv = 1 modulo q.

The first signature component is denoted r and is equal to gkx reduced modulo q. The second signature component is denoted s and is equal to (h + r * w) * kinv reduced modulo q.

For verification, the verifier computes h and the quantity sinv, the integer between zero and q such that s * sinv = 1 modulo q, then computes u = h * sinv modulo q and v = r * sinv modulo q. The verifier computes (gx, gy)^u = (gux, guy) and (gwx, gwy)^v = (gwvx, gwvy), and adds the two points, giving (sumx, sumy) = (gux, guy) + (gwvx, gwvy), where the addition is addition of points on the elliptic curve. The signature is verified if sumx modulo q equals r.
sections.plainLanguage: Signing uses a random number that is thrown away afterwards, so the same message signed twice gives two different signatures. Verification undoes the arithmetic with the public key alone, and the check succeeds when the two computations agree. The private key never leaves the signer.

sections.title: The Worked Test Vectors
sections.content:
The RFC gives a complete worked example for each of the three algorithms, using the group parameters, the static and ephemeral keys, the hash of the message abc, the resulting signature, and every intermediate value needed to verify it.

For ECDSA-256, IANA assigned the ID value 9. The example signs the message abc, whose SHA-256 hash is BA7816BF 8F01CFEA 414140DE 5DAE2223 B00361A3 96177A9C B410FF61 F20015AD. The signature is the pair r and s, and the signature is valid because the computed sumx modulo q equals r. If that signature were the one appearing in the authentication payload, the payload would begin 00000048 00090000, which is the payload length followed by the method identifier, and then carry the r and s values.
sections.plainLanguage: The document gives a full example for each algorithm, including every number an implementer needs to check their arithmetic against. The example signs the three characters abc, and the payload shows the method identifier followed by the two signature numbers.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: IANA updated its registry of IPsec authentication methods and its registry of IKEv2 authentication methods to include ECDSA-256, ECDSA-384 and ECDSA-521. The ID values assigned in this document are 9 for ECDSA-256, 10 for ECDSA-384 and 11 for ECDSA-521.
sections.plainLanguage: The three algorithms were given registry entries so that both ends of an IKE or IKEv2 exchange can name the same method by number.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Because this document proposes new digital signatures for use within IKE and IKEv2, many of the security considerations contained within the IKE and IKEv2 documents apply here as well. Implementers should ensure that appropriate security measures are in place when they deploy ECDSA within IKE or IKEv2.

ECDSA-256, ECDSA-384 and ECDSA-521 are designed to offer security comparable with AES-128, AES-192 and AES-256 respectively.
sections.plainLanguage: Everything that governs the security of IKE and IKEv2 applies to these signature methods too. The three are chosen to match the strength of the three AES key sizes.
